chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Markets Matter to Your Job

lessons.title: How Money Flows: Savers, Borrowers, Intermediaries and Markets

children.text: The last lesson established what financial markets are. This one follows the money. Every rupee that funds a factory, a working capital loan or a metro project started as somebody's savings, and it travelled through a chain of institutions to get there. Once you can see that chain, most finance news stops being abstract.

body.text: There is no separate pool of company money and household money. Your salary, your EPF contribution and your SIP are the raw material that funds Indian business. Financial markets are just the plumbing in between.

children.text: Two Sides of Every Rupee

markDefs.definition: A person or entity that earns more than it spends and therefore has money to lend or invest. Households are the largest surplus unit in India.
A person or entity that needs more money than it currently has and therefore borrows or raises capital. Companies and governments are the largest deficit units.
An institution that stands between savers and borrowers, such as a bank, mutual fund, insurance company or pension fund, pooling money from many savers and channelling it to borrowers.

children.text: In any economy, some people earn more than they spend. They are
surplus units
, and in India they are mostly households, including you. Others need more money than they have. They are
deficit units
: companies building capacity, startups funding losses, and governments funding roads and welfare. Between the two sits a layer of
financial intermediaries
whose entire business is moving money from the first group to the second, and taking a cut for the service.

body.label: Who Funds Indian Business
body.context: Indian households have long contributed the largest share of the country's gross domestic savings, well ahead of companies and government.

body.title: Where Household Financial Savings Typically Go in India (Illustrative)

body.text: Notice how little of it goes directly into shares. Most households never buy a share, yet their money still reaches the equity market through EPF, NPS, insurance policies and mutual funds. If your salary slip has an EPF deduction, you are already an equity investor in a small way.

children.text: Two Routes from Saver to Borrower

body.title: The Indirect Route vs the Direct Route

columns.label: Indirect Route (Through a Bank)
points: You deposit ₹5 lakh in an SBI fixed deposit
The bank decides who to lend it to, and you never know the borrower
Your return is fixed and contractual, whatever the borrower earns
The bank carries the credit risk, under RBI regulation
If the borrower defaults, the bank still owes you your deposit

columns.label: Direct Route (Through Markets)
points: You buy shares or bonds of a specific company on NSE or BSE
You choose the borrower and can see exactly what you own
Your return depends on how that company actually performs
You carry the risk yourself, in a market regulated by SEBI
If the company does badly, nobody reimburses you

children.text: Mutual funds sit in between. You hand money to a professional, as in the indirect route, but you bear the market risk yourself, as in the direct route. That hybrid is exactly why SEBI insists every mutual fund advertisement carries a risk warning, while your bank fixed deposit does not.
The Cast of Intermediaries

body.caption: Who Sits Between Your Savings and a Company's Bank Account

cells: Banks
Take deposits, make loans, run payments
Salary account, FD, home loan, the company's working capital limit
NBFCs
Lend without a full banking licence, often to segments banks avoid
Vehicle loan, gold loan, equipment finance, consumer EMI
Mutual funds (AMCs)
Pool money from many investors and buy shares or bonds
Your SIP, your company's surplus cash in liquid funds
Insurance companies
Collect premiums and invest the float for decades
Term plan, ULIP, group health cover from your employer
Pension funds (EPFO, NPS)
Invest long-term retirement money across bonds and equity
The EPF deduction on your salary slip, your NPS contribution
Stockbrokers
Route your buy and sell orders to the exchange
Zerodha, Groww, your bank's broking arm
Exchanges and clearing corporations
Match trades, then guarantee settlement so neither side is cheated
NSE and BSE, behind every trade you place
Depositories
Hold your shares in electronic form
NSDL and CDSL, named on your demat statement
Merchant bankers
Help companies issue shares and bonds, and price the issue
The names listed on an IPO prospectus

body.title: Who Does What?
body.question: Your company parks ₹8 crore of surplus cash in a liquid mutual fund for three weeks, before a large vendor payment. Which intermediary is now deciding which borrowers that money reaches?
options: The asset management company running the liquid fund
RBI, since the money is short-term
body.explanation: The AMC's fund manager decides what the liquid fund buys, typically very short-term debt such as treasury bills and commercial paper. A depository only holds securities, an exchange only matches trades, and RBI regulates the wider system rather than picking individual borrowers.

children.text: Follow One SIP All the Way Through
Take a ₹10,000 monthly SIP into an equity mutual fund, started by an employee in Gurugram. Here is the journey that ₹10,000 makes.

body.title: From Salary Slip to Share Ownership

events.title: Salary Credited
events.description: Your employer pays salary into your bank account. Part of your cost to company never reaches you at all: EPF goes straight to the EPFO, which invests it in government bonds, corporate bonds and equity index funds.

events.title: SIP Auto-Debit Runs
events.description: ₹10,000 leaves your bank account on the SIP date, through a mandate you signed once. Your bank has now shifted from being your borrower to being a payment pipe.

events.title: The AMC Allots Units
events.description: The asset management company receives the money and allots you units at the applicable net asset value, based on the cut-off timing rules for that fund type.

events.title: The Fund Manager Deploys It
events.description: Your ₹10,000 is pooled with money from lakhs of other investors. The fund manager buys shares on NSE or BSE, within the mandate stated in the scheme document.

events.title: The Money Reaches Another Investor
events.description: Those shares are bought from existing shareholders in the secondary market, so the money reaches a seller, not the company. This is the step almost everyone gets wrong.

events.title: The Company Finally Gets Funded
events.description: When that company issues fresh shares through an IPO, QIP or rights issue, mutual funds, insurers and pension funds are the buyers. That is the moment household savings actually become company capital.

body.text: A deep secondary market is what makes the primary market possible. Institutions will only fund a new issue if they believe they can sell those shares later without crashing the price. Liquidity today is what pays for capacity expansion tomorrow.

children.text: Nobody Moves Money for Free
Every intermediary in that chain charges for the service, and the clearest example is a bank. It pays savers one rate and charges borrowers a higher one. The gap is called the spread.

body.caption: A bank earns the spread for taking on credit risk, managing liquidity and running the operation.

body.title: Size the Bank's Cut
body.prompt: A bank takes ₹100 crore of deposits at 6.50% and lends the same ₹100 crore at 9.50%. Ignoring costs and defaults, how much does it earn in a year from the spread, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: The spread is 9.50% minus 6.50%, which is 3.00 percentage points. ₹100 crore × 3.00% = ₹3 crore a year. Out of that the bank must cover branches, staff, technology and loan losses, which is why the headline spread is not profit.

children.text: Stretch that idea across the whole system and you get one of the most useful pictures in finance: money has different prices depending on who is borrowing and how risky they look.

body.title: The Price of Money Depends on the Borrower (Illustrative Annual Rates)

children.text: The government pays least because it is the safest borrower in rupees. A credit card user pays most because the lender has no collateral and no certainty. Every rate in between is the market pricing risk. Chapter 3 goes into how those rates are actually set.

body.title: We Are Profitable, So Why Do We Borrow?
body.scenario: You manage operations at a profitable Coimbatore textile firm with steady annual profits. In a town hall, a colleague from the plant asks the CFO why the company keeps a ₹30 crore bank limit open and is now talking to investors, when the company makes money every year.
body.prompt: How would you explain it in plain language?
body.modelAnswer: Profit and cash are not the same thing, and neither is the same as capital. First, timing: the firm pays for cotton, wages and power months before customers pay their invoices, so it needs working capital to bridge that gap even in a great year. Second, scale: a new spinning line might cost ₹60 crore, which is several years of profit. Funding it from profits alone means arriving late to the opportunity, so the firm borrows or raises equity and pays for that capital out of the returns the new line generates. Third, cost: if the firm earns more on the investment than the interest it pays, borrowing raises shareholder returns rather than reducing them. Fourth, resilience: keeping an unused bank limit open is insurance, because the cheapest time to arrange credit is when you do not urgently need it. The trade-off is that debt must be serviced whatever happens, which is exactly why the CFO watches the interest rates set in the markets we are studying.

body.title: What Happens When the Plumbing Blocks: IL&FS, 2018

children.text: In September 2018, IL&FS, a large infrastructure financier that was widely assumed to be safe, defaulted on its debt payments. It had been funding long-term infrastructure projects with short-term borrowings that needed constant refinancing. The chain reaction showed how tightly connected the plumbing is:
Debt mutual funds holding IL&FS paper took losses, and investors who assumed debt funds were safe redeemed in a hurry.
Those funds were major buyers of NBFC commercial paper, so when they stopped buying, healthy NBFCs suddenly could not roll over their own borrowings either.
NBFCs that could not borrow stopped lending, which hit vehicle finance, developer loans and small business credit for months.
Borrowers with no connection to IL&FS found their sanctioned limits shrinking, purely because one link in the chain broke.

The lesson for a non finance manager is simple. When you hear that credit markets have tightened, it is not abstract news. It shows up as a customer paying late, a vendor demanding advances, or your own expansion plan being deferred.

body.title: Trace Your Own Money This Week
steps: Open your latest salary slip and note the EPF deduction, because that money is already invested in bonds and equity index funds by the EPFO
Check one bank statement and mark which entries are you saving, which are you borrowing, and which are just payments
Log in to your demat or mutual fund account and note which depository, NSDL or CDSL, holds your shares
Pick one fund you own and read the top ten holdings in its factsheet, so you know which companies your savings actually fund
Ask your finance team one question: does our company borrow from banks, from the bond market, or both

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: An institution that pools money from many savers and channels it to borrowers, taking a cut for the service, is called a financial ___.
body.explanation: Banks, NBFCs, mutual funds, insurance companies and pension funds are all financial intermediaries. The direct route, where you buy a company's shares or bonds yourself, is the one that skips them, though even then a broker, an exchange and a depository are involved in executing the trade.

points: Money flows from surplus units, mainly households, to deficit units, mainly companies and government, through a chain of intermediaries
The indirect route runs through banks, which carry the credit risk and pay you a fixed return; the direct route runs through markets, where you pick the borrower and carry the risk yourself
Most Indian households reach the equity market without buying a single share, through EPF, NPS, insurance and mutual funds
A SIP buys shares from other investors in the secondary market, so household savings become company capital only when the company issues fresh securities
Every intermediary charges for the service, and the price of money rises with the risk of the borrower, from government bonds at the bottom to credit card dues at the top
When one link breaks, as in the IL&FS default of 2018, credit dries up even for borrowers who had nothing to do with the original problem

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment or financial advice. All rates, savings splits and figures shown are illustrative, meant to teach the mechanics rather than to state current market levels. Institution names are used only as examples.
